Messages.Author: Alan Quin
Messages.Body:
It may be that I am attempting the impossible, yet I believe that there is a
way for the Gangrel to become a resonable political force. As the Gangrel are not as adept at politics as other clans, their approach to politics requires
a little not-so-subtle manipulation of the field.
It is paramount to get Angus into play, so this approach cannot always be used, but his three votes are vital. With no princes, gangrels are giving up
the political high-ground to Ventrue or Malkavian. This can be re-taken by
force. Eliminating opposing vote-winners through direct attacks, sending them to torpor before proposing votes of your own gives the wolf boys and girls a
suprising amount of political get up and go.
I have gained a reasonable amount of success with this, and it gives
my gangrels another dimension to their game. They still rather engague in
combat, but adding a little politics stops them being predictable. Has anyone
else tried this approach?
"The Naturally Talented" Gangrel.
Alan.

>distribute up to n of that blood (n=number of methuselahs in game) as

Because they could have (and IMO positively /should/ have) said this
in a perfectly unambiguous manner: `/his/ blood', if your
interpretation is the intended one. As it stands, `that blood'
is ambiguous, with two interpretations possible.

WotC has serious problems of this sort: unable to represent
the rules in a precise manner. IMO they have something to
learn from AH. If WotC wants to make a lot of money, they
better put in the effort so that they (to some degree, at
least) deserve it.

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
pech...@lvl-sun676.usc.edu (gomi no sensei) writes:

>In article <3latue$m...@sif.cs.cornell.edu>,

>Alan Kwan <kw...@cs.cornell.edu> wrote:

>>be able to reduce his pool below your own ...

>I don't see how you're arriving at that; the text of parity shift reads
>in part: "select a methuselah with more blood in pool than yourself, then
>distribute up to n of that blood (n=number of methuselahs in game) as
>you see fit."

>I mean, I can see how one could think that 'that blood' referred to the
>shifted player's excess over the vote-caller, but it's stretching the

>wording a bit to say so, IMO. It seems apparent (in this area, anyhow)
>to reapportion blood from the general pool of the shifted player, and to
>check for higher pool only as a condition for calling the vote in the first
>place.

There is no official answer to this question, even though I've asked it
many times on this group. Tom Wylie e-mailed me a guess (along the
lines that it would be as gomi no sensei says), but made it clear that it
could go either way.

The name (Parity shift) leads me to believe it would be as Alan Kwan says:
if you have 5 and your Prey has 7, then you can only move 2 (7-5) blood
around (up to the number of Methuselah's in the game, which I'm assuming
is at least two :-). That's what parity shift means.

Note that this is not a good argument for WotC, since they frequently
overrun the card name with illogical rulings (Rotschreck and re-Rotschreck).

L. Scott

It would be clear if it said "his blood", but it says "that blood", which
is vague. I'm awareit is hard to oust people with any vote, but compare
it to other votes. No other vote can do any substantial pool loss without
hurting other players, and even Conservative agitation will have to have
significant harm to other players to get it to pass if you haven't run off
with the Camarilla. With unlimited Parity Shift, you can pass it by
pribing other voting Methuselehs, so it becomes something that can hurt
another player a LOT (more than any other vote, typically) without having
to hurt anybody else in the process (which typically makes votes fail, as
even 1 pool loss makes a Methuseleh get very defensive). This conflicts
with the usual restrictions on votes.

Admittedly, the word "parity" does tend to suggest equality but I think
you're making a fundamental mistake here by trying to suggest that this
situation is comparable to some of the more bizarre MtG rulings WotC has
issued. First of all, the full title is Parity _Shift_ which can quite
arguably refer to a "shift towards parity", involving no guarantee that such
a shift might not fall short or overshoot the mark. It does not automatically
suggest the full implementation of parity, as you seem to want it to.
Secondly, there's no particular rule that a card name needs to be accurately
descriptive of what it does. For all we know, it's named after a fictional
character named "Parity", who was fond of robbing from the rich past the point
of sanity (in the manner of Dennis Moore, perhaps, but in terms of blood
rather than Lupens). You gotta read the _text_ to see what the card does...

>>
>> L. Scott
>
> I had my girlfriend look at Parity Shift for me in order to try and
>figure it out after a conflict in interpretations. She is an English
>graduate, and she and I would both agree with L. Scott on this one. As
>Parity _Shift_, it makes sense to only move that amount that is in
>difference. If you decide to moving the number in the game, no matter
>what the difference is, it turns into Parity _Landslide_. The card is
>meant as an equalizer, not a killer.

Whoa. I'm confused. The card text looks quite clear to me. It states
how to use the card ("Select a Methuselah who has more blood in his
or her pool than you.") and then describes what it does. The description
of what it does says not a thing about the differential in any two blood
pools. So where does your English grad girl friend find a reference to such
a differential on the card?!?

The description clearly defines the meaning of the '#' symbol on the card.
Maybe someone will enlighten me here but I just don't see the source of
confusion here.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams) writes:

>It would be clear if it said "his blood", but it says "that blood", which
>is vague.

I disagree. The term "that blood" clearly refers to the (selected) subject's
blood pool, which had been referred to previously. It does NOT refer to
"the differential between the subject's blood pool and the acting Meth's
blood pool" because that concept was never mentioned in the first place.
I think you all are making an unconcious but unwarranted jump here, from
the use of the inequality in the statement that determines which Meth you're
allowed to use as a subject of the vote (on the one hand) to the calculation
of this differential (on the other). The two are not the same thing.

If there is something that's unclear here, it's what happens when '#' is
greater than the amount of blood in the subject's blood pool. Should you
reduce '#' to equal that amount of blood or are you simply not allowed to
select that Meth for this vote. Neither answer is obvious to me.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams) writes:

>fre...@anthrax.cisco.com (Frederick Scott)
>
>>curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams) writes:
>
>>>It would be clear if it said "his blood", but it says "that blood",
>which
>>>is vague.
>
>>I disagree. The term "that blood" clearly refers to the (selected)
>subject's
>>blood pool, which had been referred to previously. It does NOT refer to
>>"the differential between the subject's blood pool and the acting Meth's
>>blood pool" because that concept was never mentioned in the first place.
>

>"Select a Methuselah who has more blood in his or her pool than you.
>Divide up to # of that blood among the Methuselahs' blood pools as you see
>fit."
>

>More blood = that blood.

Correct - "that blood"...his blood pool...the _whole_ thing.

The word "more" in this usage is an adjective that describes a relationship
with something else (the other blood pool, your blood pool, in this case). It
does not refer to the _difference_ between the two, as you seem to be
suggesting.

If I handed you $100 and you said you wanted more money, then you would be
speaking about the difference because "more money" would refer to another
amount beyond what you already had.

But if I owed you $100 and proposed to give you "more money than that"
and you agreed that that would be nice, I had better not hand you ONLY a $5
bill and say that I had given you "more money than $100". "More" in this case
refers to the _whole_ amount: $105. Likewise with the "more blood" in Parity
Shift.

Fred

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <1995Apr13.1...@ac.dal.ca>,

Dennis Jeffery Murphy <ti...@is.dal.ca> wrote:
>: >More blood = that blood.
>
>: To me, "his or her pool" = "that blood." It's ambiguous.
>
>What's ambiguous?

Whether "that blood" means "more blood" or "his or her pool".
If many people cannot all come up with the same meaning given the
wording on the card, then the wording on the card is unclear or
misleading, which is one of the definitions of the word ambiguous.

You may think that you know what the card means (I know that I
certainly do), but from the empirical evidence, it seems that the
wording on the card is ambiguous.
